France’s fiscal crisis is nearing its breaking point

With debt approaching 120% of GDP and borrowing costs rising, France faces mounting pressure to rein in its deficit, but pension reform and spending cuts remain politically fraught ahead of the 2027 election, The Editorial Board writes for Bloomberg.

Bloomberg Editors

20 October, 2026 04:43 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

F rance’s crisis keeps getting more extreme, spilling over the weekend into broader protests that precipitated hundreds of millions of euros in damage and nearly 2,400 arrests. The country’s leaders are rightly focused on curtailing the violence. Yet as they seek ways to placate a frustrated populace, they must be careful not to make a bad fiscal situation worse.

It’s hard to overstate how dire France’s finances have become, particularly now that worried investors have pushed its 10-year bond yields to almost 5%. If borrowing costs remain this high, the interest rate the government pays will soon exceed the economy’s nominal growth rate. As a result, just stabilizing sovereign debt — currently about 120% of gross domestic product, among the highest in Europe — could require running a sustained primary budget surplus of as much as 2% of GDP. That’s a feat France hasn’t achieved since the 1970s.

The politics of achieving the necessary deficit reduction, estimated to be at least €125 billion by 2032, could hardly be more fraught. Among potential savings and revenue measures, pension reform stands out: Increasing the retirement age to 65 — still below the norm among western European peers — could reap about €18 billion. Yet when President Emmanuel Macron in 2023 pushed through an (ultimately postponed) increase from 62 to 64, the move triggered some of the country’s largest-ever protests — albeit rivaled in violence by the weekend’s events — and contributed to the far-right National Rally party’s success in 2024 elections.

Show Full Article

With presidential elections coming next year, there’s even less appetite for prudence. The current minority government’s 2027 budget proposal, which would reduce the deficit by about €28 billion, faces stiff opposition. National Rally’s Marine Le Pen, who leads national polling for the next presidential election, sought to calm bond markets with a pledge of fiscal consolidation that contrasts sharply with the tax cuts and spending promises in her platform. Meanwhile, left-wing candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, whose statements have been blamed for inflaming protesters, proposed simply canceling more than €500 billion in French public debt held by its central bank — an absurdity that, even if possible, would serve only to spook markets more.

Eventually, the nation’s leaders will have to recognize that there’s no alternative to boring, unpleasant budget discipline. The longer that takes, the greater the damage will be.

France’s malaise places it on a collision course with the broader European Union. The longer it delays serious reform, the more precarious its finances will become as it takes on more debt at higher yields. If investors ultimately refuse to lend, the EU and the European Central Bank will face a dilemma: Organize a bailout or let the bloc’s second-largest economy descend into financial chaos. The best-case scenario would entail imposing austerity measures on France potentially harsher than what’s now needed to stabilize its debt. The worst would be an acute crisis involving a French default, bank runs and possibly a breakup of the euro.

If France’s current minority government can’t act, hopefully the next election will produce leadership capable of delivering the difficult reform the country needs. Even populists have been known to act responsibly when confronted with the immutable facts of public finance. There’s no better way out.

Why US satellites are so crucial to Ukraine’s defence, and why Kyiv can’t look to Europe for help

Kyiv’s reliance on US tech reemerged as a vulnerability mid-October. Around the same time, sudden restrictions were reported on SpaceX Starlink satellite services used by Ukraine.

Gerry Doyle

20 October, 2026 03:30 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

A model of a Gen4 ICEYE satellite at the companys headquarters in Espoo, Finland.

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

Ukraine’s defense against Russian attacks depends heavily on US satellites, not only for warning of incoming missiles but also for the communications that keep drones and frontline forces operating.

European nations are trying to catch up with the US in space-based intelligence and connectivity, but still lack many crucial capabilities that underpin Ukrainian combat operations and missile-defense systems.

Kyiv’s reliance on American technology and support reemerged as a vulnerability in mid-October, when President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine had not received the usual warning from allies of ballistic missile launches before a deadly attack on the country. Around the same time, sudden restrictions were reported on SpaceX Starlink satellite services used by Ukrainian forces.

Show Full Article

Why are US satellites so important for Ukraine?

Starlink — the low-earth orbit commercial satellite communication network established by Elon Musk’s SpaceX — and its military version, Starshield, have come to underpin the Ukrainian armed forces’ command infrastructure after terrestrial communications were badly damaged by Russian strikes early in the war. The ground terminals allow pilots of Ukrainian interceptor drones and mid-range strike drones to control the machines, while the network also allows ground forces to coordinate supplies and movements along the front line.

US military satellites are also vital for Ukraine’s defense against Russian missiles and drones.

No country beside the US can offer near-constant space-based imaging of Europe. Its numerous and powerful spy satellites can provide high-quality images, including video. Via the Space Based Infrared System, or SBIRS, the US also has satellites in geosynchronous orbit, which keeps them over one spot on earth. These are the backbone of US early warning for missiles anywhere on Earth, and there is no equivalent in Europe. The satellites allow for real-time tracking of cruise missiles and other low-flying weapons that might escape detection by ground radar until it’s too late to stop them. This is especially helpful for a military, such as Ukraine’s, that relies on drones, aircraft cannons and other low-tech methods of destroying swarms of mass-produced projectiles.

SBIRS can also detect the launch plumes of ballistic missiles. These missiles travel much faster and higher than other airborne weapons, making them harder to deal with. Knowing when a ballistic missile is fired, its speed and direction is vital for Ukraine’s air-raid warning systems. (An alert — even one that comes a minute or two ahead of the impact — can save lives by giving civilians time to take cover).

That capability also gives Ukraine’s armed forces a greater chance of intercepting and destroying the inbound weapons. It can be harder to knock out a missile at longer range. But a miss at long range still allows time for another shot. If an incoming missile is only noticed at the last minute, a miss at close range blows the final chance to foil a potentially devastating attack.

How were these capabilities disrupted recently?

Ukrainian officials said the US government did not send early warning alerts ahead of some recent Russian ballistic missile attacks on the country.

Ukraine also complained that drones equipped with Starlink terminals were losing connectivity when traveling at speeds above 161 kilometers (100 miles) per hour in Ukraine. The drones often need to travel faster than this to intercept an incoming Russian drone traveling at 400 kilometers per hour, and the restrictions have disrupted drone interceptions and mid-range strikes.

Asked who ordered the change, President Zelenskyy pointed to “the authorities, the White House,” citing “sources” he didn’t identify. A senior US official has said Trump didn’t order any limitations.

How does Europe use its satellites to help Ukraine?

Europe’s militaries have a variety of earth-observation satellites that help Ukrainian forces locate Russian troops, tanks, artillery and military installations and identify ammunition depots, airfields and missile-launch facilities. The Ukrainian military can use that information to strike at those facilities.

Finland’s ICEYE synthetic-aperture radar satellites can operate at night and see through cloud cover, smoke and haze. French satellite sensors detect thermal radiation and identify human activity that conventional cameras can easily miss.

Germany has paid commercial satellite companies such as US-based Planet Labs for high-resolution imagery for Ukraine, including inside Russian territory. This can provide data for targeting and spotting Russian military movement over time — potentially crucial intelligence that could thwart an attempted attack.

When might Europe close the intelligence gap?

Europe is under heavy pressure to stop relying on the US for its own defense, and military budgets in the region are growing again for the first time since the Cold War. A chunk of that new spending is going toward “strategic enablers” — communications and other systems that have an outsized impact on warfare despite not being weapons. European nations are racing to put more satellites in orbit and get more surveillance aircraft in the air.

The European Union has begun launching the first of nearly 350 Iris2 secure communications satellites. ICEYE recently signed a deal with Nokia to develop a secure communications constellation for European defense and security. Airbus SE has for decades built satellites, and German defense giant Rheinmetall AG has also entered the game, including through a partnership with ICEYE.

The pace of the rollout is limited, however, as the region does not have enough rockets with the power to launch heavy military satellites into orbit. Europe’s only sovereign heavy rocket booster is Ariane 6, which launches about 10 times a year from Kourou in French Guyana on the northern coast of South America. And European governments want to avoid using SpaceX as they prefer to find their own way into orbit.

So could Europe eventually match the US for space-based intelligence?

No existing or currently planned European service could match the scale and capability of Starlink. The closest existing European equivalent is OneWeb, a system of around 600 satellites operated by France’s Eutelsat. Starlink satellites orbit at an altitude of around 550 km, around half that of OneWeb’s network. This makes for shorter signal transmission delays — a crucial factor with time-critical military systems. The 10,000-satellite Starlink network also offers greater data capacity and better ground coverage, and its terminals are smaller so they can be mounted more easily on drones.

When it comes to military observation satellites, there’s no European plan to match the capability of US SBIRS. The US has nearly 250 military satellites in orbit, compared with about 150 for China and about 100 for Russia. Many more are considered dual-use.

Europe as a whole has about 50.

Besides imagery, US satellites can intercept communications and other transmissions — so-called “signals intelligence” that can also be used on the battlefield.

The US Space Force also announced in September that it had placed an operational weapon in orbit, although officials declined to say what sort of system it was.

–With assistance from Michael Nienaber and Volodymyr Verbianyi.

Zelenskyy travels to Oslo for new peace talks as pressure mounts from US to reach a deal with Russia

US envoy Steve Witkoff is expected in Oslo to take part in the talks with Norwegian Pm Jonas Gahr Støre and Finland’s President Alexander Stubb. Jared Kushner will take part online.

Olesia Safronova

20 October, 2026 03:19 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Volodymyr Zelenskyy in London on Oct. 14. Photographer: Betty Laura Zapata/Bloomberg

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is traveling to Norway for new peace talks as US pressure mounts for concessions from Kyiv to reach a deal with Russia.

US envoy Steve Witkoff is expected in Oslo to take part in the talks on Tuesday with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finland’s President Alexander Stubb, according to a government statement in Norway. Another US envoy, Jared Kushner, will take part online in the talks, the statement said.

The meeting’s being held amid escalating tensions between Zelenskyy and Donald Trump. The American president reiterated criticism of the Ukrainian leader on Monday after officials in Kyiv said they suspect the US is intermittently restricting intelligence sharing despite denials from Washington, allowing Russian missiles to strike Ukraine without warning.

Show Full Article

Zelenskyy “doesn’t know what he’s talking about” and should have settled the war a long time ago, Trump told reporters. “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. They’ve given us nothing.”

Relations between Trump and Zelenskyy have soured since the US announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin this month for diesel supplies to American and global markets as the White House strives to cut surging fuel prices ahead of Nov. 3 midterm elections.

Trump followed that up by deferring sweeping new sanctions targeting Russian energy sales. That sparked criticism from lawmakers including in his own Republican party that he was helping Russia to continue financing the war that Putin started in February 2022.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in an interview with Bloomberg on Monday that Putin is seeking not only to defeat Ukraine, but to also undermine democracy in Europe. The key condition in the war was Ukraine’s territorial integrity “and that is not to dispute,” he said.

“I’m trying to convince Donald Trump each time I’m meeting him that this should be in his own interest,” Merz said. “A stable Europe, European continent, European Union as a partner in the world is something which is worthwhile for the Americans as well.”

The Ukrainian leader spoke by video call with Witkoff and Kushner, who is Trump’s son-in-law, on Sunday to discuss the war and possibilities for new talks. Zelenskyy said in a Bloomberg News interview on Sunday that the US side also planned to meet with Putin.

A Russian strike involving 16 ballistic missiles overnight on Sunday and Monday was the third time in the same week in which Ukraine was left without the usual advance warning it receives from US intelligence about incoming attacks. Ukraine has also accused the US of restricting access to SpaceX’s Starshield satellite technology.

How US Satellites Became Crucial to Ukraine’s Defense: Explainer

Zelenskyy said Tuesday he held “constructive” talks with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio about ballistic missile interceptors, early warning on attacks and the situation with Starshield “which needs to be restored.” They agreed to be in contact soon for an update, he said in a post on social media.

US officials have rebuffed accusations of any slowdown in intelligence to Ukraine. Trump last week said he didn’t order limitations on Ukraine’s access to Starshield.

Trump said Monday that “somebody else” instead of Zelenskyy should negotiate on behalf of Ukraine. He told reporters that “Russia frankly has been fine on Ukraine — they haven’t been doing much.”

(Updates with German chancellor in the seventh, eighth paragraphs. An earlier version of this story corrected the date to Tuesday in what is now the 11th paragraph.)

Wearing headphones during surgery linked to lower risk of nausea, vomiting – China study

The trial involved 192 adults aged 18 to 65, all of whom underwent surgery under general anaesthesia.

Purvi Rajpuria

20 October, 2026 01:47 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Akio Kon | Bloomberg

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Wearing noise-cancelling headphones during minimally invasive gynaecological surgery can lower the risk of post-operative nausea and vomiting (PONV), a recent clinical trial has found. The findings were presented at the ANESTHESIOLOGY® 2026 annual meeting held between October 16 and 20.

While anaesthetic and pain medications are well-known contributors to PONV, researchers say noise in the operating room may also be a lesser-known factor.

A common and unpleasant side effect after surgery, PONV can lead to dehydration, delayed recovery, increased medication use and longer stays in the recovery room.

Show Full Article

These symptoms are common in patients undergoing minimally invasive gynaecological surgery under general anaesthesia, even when they receive medication to prevent them.

Noise in the operating room  The trial involved 192 adults aged 18 to 65, all of whom underwent surgery under general anaesthesia. They were randomly assigned to one of two groups.

One group wore over-the-head noise-cancelling headphones from the start of anaesthesia until the surgery ended, while the other did not. All patients received the same general anaesthesia and medication to prevent PONV.

Within 48 hours of surgery, 35.4 per cent of patients who wore headphones experienced PONV, compared with 52.1 per cent of those who did not. Patients wearing headphones therefore had a 32 per cent lower relative risk of nausea and vomiting.

This translates to about 17 fewer cases of PONV for every 100 patients who wore headphones. Patients in the headphone group also experienced less severe PONV within the first 24 hours after surgery.

No adverse side effects were reported among those who wore headphones.

Also Read: Walking before cancer surgery can cut risk of postoperative delirium by 50%, finds study

Sound processing under anaesthesia The operating room had an average sound level of about 66 decibels, somewhere between the sound of a normal conversation and that of a nearby vacuum cleaner.

Researchers noted that while patients under anaesthesia may not be consciously aware of these sounds, their bodies may still process them.

“Our findings suggest that simply reducing intraoperative noise could give anesthesiologists another tool to help prevent PONV after surgery, without adding another medication,” said Huayue Liu, MD, lead author of the study and an anesthesiologist at the First Affiliated Hospital of Soochow University in Suzhou, China.

“Future studies should measure the amount of noise patients are exposed to during surgery and how their brains and bodies respond to better understand whether and how sound may affect PONV,” Liu added.

(Edited by Maryam Hassan)
